name: Viana do Castelo
title: Ship Thickness Measurement in Viana do Castelo | UTM Gauging
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging at Viana do Castelo, Portugal: newbuild and repair-yard hull checks, coasters, fishing vessels and tugs, tank and deck UTM.
h1: Viana do Castelo Ship Gauging for Yard Work and Short-Sea Tonnage
intro: Viana do Castelo sits where the Lima meets the Atlantic in northern Portugal, a small commercial port with a long shipbuilding history and a yard that still builds and refits vessels today. Visiting ships are mostly coasters, bulkers and workboats, and the yard adds ferries, tugs and passenger craft. Our ultrasonic thickness gauging technicians travel from India to the ship for each job, measuring hull, tanks and decks at the quay or in the yard.

highlights.h: A working shipyard on the Lima
highlights.p: The yard at Viana builds and repairs ships, so gauging can follow its programme: baseline readings on new structure, wastage checks on refits, and measured steel lists drawn up before a repair is specified.

Coasters, workboats and fishing vessels spend short periods alongside. We plan compact gauging runs around cargo work and crew changes, concentrating on ballast tanks, deck plating and the shell at the waterline.
Entry over the Lima bar depends on swell and tide, and ships arrive on its schedule. Our plans keep slack for late arrivals so technicians are not left waiting on a ship that cannot cross.

port.h: The Lima estuary, the port and its traffic
p: Viana do Castelo lies on the north bank of the Lima estuary, close to the Spanish border, with the hills of the Santa Luzia peninsula standing above the town. The commercial port occupies the estuary's lower reach and is sheltered by breakwaters, but the approach crosses a bar where Atlantic swell builds in winter. Pilotage and tides decide when larger vessels can enter, and ships awaiting a favourable window hold off the coast rather than inside the river. The character of the place is that of a modest regional harbour rather than a hub, with a handful of deep-water berths for ships and a separate fishing and leisure area.

Visiting traffic is mainly short-sea. Coasters bring and take general cargo, wood products, cereals and other bulk, and some project cargo for the region's industries moves over the quay. Components for wind turbines, including long blades produced in the area, give the port a specialist niche that calls for heavy-lift gear and careful stowage. Tugs, pilot boats, fishing vessels, research craft and coastal workboats complete the picture, with passenger vessels and small expedition-style ships appearing as the yard completes new tonnage. Cruise calls are infrequent and small.

That mix means gauging at Viana is largely a matter of fitting around quick turnarounds and yard programmes. Ships seldom stay long enough for a full survey scope alongside, so the sensible work is targeted: ballast tanks, forepeak and aft peak, hatch coamings, deck plating and the shell at the waterline, where wastage concentrates on older coasters that have worked the Biscay and Iberian coasts for decades. Fishing vessels and tugs are inspected when the owner has laid them up or hauled them for maintenance, and yard newbuilds are gauged to record the as-built condition of plating before delivery.

facilities.h: Where gauging takes place at Viana do Castelo
p: The shipyard on the Lima's north bank is the main place a ship can be gauged properly. It is the successor to the old state yard, ENVC, and today trades as West Sea; it builds and repairs vessels and has a dry dock and fitting-out quays. When a ship is docked there, the bottom and side shell are accessible, which is the natural moment for renewal-survey or condition readings. Newbuilds and conversions are also measured during fitting-out, and readings taken afloat at the quay feed back into the yard's steel planning.

Away from the yard, gauging happens alongside at the commercial quay, at a lay-by berth or on a fishing vessel's own quay. Cargo holds on a coaster can be measured during discharge once the stevedores have cleared them, and ballast tanks are accessible whenever the chief officer can release them and the enclosed-space permit is in place. Anchorage work off the bar is not realistic because of the swell and the difficulty of boarding. For a ship that needs a larger dock than the yard can offer, owners usually look to Vigo or Leixões, and readings taken at Viana can go ahead to the repair port as a steel list.
list: West Sea shipyard on the Lima — newbuild and refit gauging, and dry-dock readings of shell and tanks
Yard fitting-out quays — hull, tank and deck readings on ferries, tugs and passenger craft before delivery
Commercial quay — hold, hatch coaming and ballast tank gauging on coasters and bulkers during discharge
Lay-by berths in the river — deck and shell readings on workboats and tugs between contracts
Fishing vessel quays — hull and tank gauging on trawlers and longliners during maintenance stops
Repair berths for onward docking — pre-docking steel lists prepared for yards at Vigo or Leixões

context.h: Portuguese port state control and the yard's regulatory setting
p: Port state control in Portugal follows the Paris MoU, and inspections at Viana are carried out by the national maritime authority, the Direção-Geral de Recursos Naturais, Segurança e Serviços Marítimos (DGRM). The port sees fewer foreign-flag calls than the big ports, but coasters from older fleets turn up regularly, and such ships are those most often selected for inspection. A measured set of thickness readings before the call is a useful way for a manager to know what condition the structure is in before an inspector sees it.

Ships built or converted in Viana come under the rules of whichever class society is classing the project, and the thickness readings that matter at delivery are those that establish the original plate thickness for later comparison. For ships already trading, the EU Ship Recycling Regulation requires an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on board vessels calling at EU ports, and the EU emissions trading system has covered shipping since 2024, with FuelEU Maritime added from 2025. Older coasters and workboats serving the region often face a decision between a steel renewal programme and replacement, and independent thickness readings give an owner the data for that choice.

jobs.h: Typical gauging jobs at Viana do Castelo
jobs.p: Work at Viana is led by the yard and by small-ship owners. A superintendent or yard planner sends the drawings and the last survey report, we agree which compartments to measure and which can be made available, and the technicians travel from India once the stay is confirmed. Because stays are short, the scope is kept compact and a priority order is agreed so the most important structure is measured first. Typical requests include:
list: As-built thickness readings on deck and bottom plating of a ferry or passenger craft nearing delivery from the yard, to give the owner a baseline record.
Ballast tank and forepeak gauging on an older coaster discharging at the commercial quay, ahead of an intermediate survey.
Shell and tank readings on a tug laid up in the river, supporting an owner's decision on steel renewal before it is put back to work.
Hatch coaming and deck plating readings on a general cargo ship carrying turbine components, where heavy-lift loading has stressed local structure.
A pre-docking steel list for a fishing vessel that will go on to a yard at Vigo, taken alongside so the repair quotation reflects measured plate.

logistics: The nearest international airport is Porto's Francisco Sá Carneiro, from which Viana is reached by road or rail; some technicians route through Lisbon instead. The ship's agent arranges ISPS access to the commercial quay, and the yard issues its own passes for work inside it. Portugal is in the Schengen area, so each technician needs a visa obtained in India, applied for once the ship's stay or dock date is firm and supported by an invitation naming the vessel. Dates on small-ship calls shift often, so travel is booked late.
vessels: Coasters and short-sea general cargo ships

faqs.q: Is there a shipyard at Viana do Castelo where ships can be docked?
faqs.a: Yes. The yard on the Lima, formerly ENVC and now trading as West Sea, builds and repairs vessels and has a dry dock. Its capacity suits ferries, tugs and mid-sized ships rather than large tankers or bulkers. For a bigger ship we take readings alongside here and pass the steel list to a larger yard, usually at Vigo or Leixões.

faqs.q: Can a ship be gauged at anchor off the Lima bar?
faqs.a: Not realistically. Atlantic swell makes boarding unsafe for much of the year, and ships waiting for the bar usually stand well offshore. Gauging is done alongside, at a lay-by berth or in the yard, where access is controlled and the ship is steady enough for readings and enclosed-space entry.

faqs.q: How do you gauge a coaster that only stays a short time alongside?
faqs.a: We agree a priority list in advance, typically ballast tanks, peaks, deck plating and hatch coamings, and start with the compartments the chief officer can release first. A compact programme finished before sailing is more useful to a superintendent than a long one left incomplete, and the report shows exactly what was and was not measured.

faqs.q: Can you take readings on new construction at the yard?
faqs.a: Yes. Readings on plating at fitting-out record the as-built thickness, which gives an owner a baseline for the ship's whole life. We agree the compartments and points with the owner's representative and the yard's quality department, and report compartment by compartment so the data can sit with the ship's survey file.

faqs.q: Does swell or weather affect scheduling at Viana?
faqs.a: It can. Winter swell on the bar delays arrivals and sailings, and ships may arrive hours or days away from their estimate. We keep the plan flexible and confirm travel as late as visa timing allows, so the team reaches a ship that is actually alongside and ready.
